question.text: What is a 'butterfly spread' and what market view does it express?

answer.text: Buy 1 lower strike option + sell 2 middle strike options + buy 1 higher strike option (all same type) — it profits when the underlying stays near the middle strike at expiry, expressing a view that the underlying will not move much
A strategy involving three different underlying assets
Buying and selling the same option at different times
A spread using weekly and monthly options simultaneously

explanation.text: The Logic: NISM Series I pages 114-116 describe a long call butterfly as buying one lower-strike call (K1), selling two middle-strike calls (K2) and buying one higher-strike call (K3), with equal spacing between the strikes (K2 - K1 = K3 - K2). The payoff is maximised when the underlying expires at the middle strike K2, so the strategy expresses a neutral, low-volatility view on the underlying. The Trap: A butterfly uses options on a single underlying at three strike prices, not three different underlyings. It is a multi-leg position established together, not the same option traded across different times. Combining weekly and monthly options is a calendar strategy, not a butterfly. Note: The four-leg structure (1:-2:1) and the equal-strike-spacing requirement are taken from Series I pages 114-116, which is also where the maximum-payoff-near-the-middle-strike behaviour is described.
